title: SQL injection: how it works, why parameterised queries are the only real fix
story:
A query is built by joining fixed text to something a user supplied. The database receives one string and has no way of knowing which parts came from the program and which came from a stranger — so if the stranger's contribution contains characters the query language treats as structure rather than content, the stranger has written part of the query.

That is the whole vulnerability, and it is worth stating at that level because the examples make it look like a problem about quote marks. It is not. It is that instruction and data were combined into one string, after which nothing downstream can separate them again. Everything else follows.

The classic demonstrations make the shape concrete. A value chosen to close the quoted section early and append a condition that is always true turns a lookup for one record into a lookup that matches every record. A value chosen to terminate the statement and begin another turns a read into whatever the attacker prefers, including a destructive one. The trailing comment marker exists so the rest of the original query, now stranded, does not cause a syntax error. None of these require anything exotic; they require the characters the language uses for structure.

The response that fails is filtering. Strip the dangerous characters, reject input matching a pattern of known attacks, escape what looks risky. This is appealing because it can be added to an existing system without changing how queries are built, and it fails for a reason that does not depend on how good the filter is.

A filter has to enumerate what is dangerous. The attacker only has to find one thing it did not enumerate, and the search space is large: alternative encodings, different character sets, case variations, nesting that survives one pass of replacement, and constructs specific to a particular database that the filter's author never saw. Every filter is a claim to have thought of everything, tested by people whose entire job is finding the exception. And a filter that is nearly perfect provides nearly no protection, because one working input is all that is required.

The fix that works does not improve the filter. It removes the situation the filter was compensating for.

With a parameterised query, the query text is sent to the database with placeholders where values go, and the values are sent separately. The database parses and plans the statement before the values are attached, so by the time they arrive the structure is already decided. A value containing a quote, a semicolon or an entire statement cannot change anything, because there is nothing left to change — it is data being placed into a slot in a plan that already exists.

Notice why this is a different kind of solution. Filtering tries to detect a hostile value. Parameterisation makes hostility irrelevant, because the value is never in a position to be interpreted. The first is a judgement that can be wrong; the second is a structural property that holds for every input including the ones nobody imagined.

Two limits matter, since parameterisation is often treated as total. It protects values, not structure — a table or column name, or a sort direction, cannot be a parameter, so code that builds those from input is still vulnerable and must select from a fixed set of allowed values instead of passing anything through. And it is only in force where it is used; one query built by joining strings, anywhere in the system, is sufficient, so this is a property of the least careful line rather than of the codebase.

The general principle is worth carrying beyond databases, because it recurs everywhere: the fix for mixing instructions with data is never better inspection of the data. It is an interface where the two cannot be mixed. Where such an interface does not exist — as with a language model receiving one sequence of text — the problem does not have a clean solution, and that is precisely because the structural separation is missing rather than because nobody has written a good enough filter.

problem.name: Instructions mixed with data
problem.shape: A command is constructed by combining program text with a value from outside.
tell: a query is assembled by joining strings
input is being escaped or stripped before use
a blocklist of dangerous patterns exists
a table or column name comes from a request
problem.move: Send the statement and the values separately, so the database plans the statement before any value is attached. Where something cannot be a parameter — a table name, a sort direction — select it from a fixed set of permitted values rather than passing input through.
problem.invariant: Once instruction and data are combined into one string, nothing downstream can separate them. Parameterisation keeps them apart so the values arrive after the structure is already decided.
problem.breaks: It protects values and not structure, so identifiers and ordering built from input remain vulnerable and need an allowed-values list instead. And it holds only where it is used — one query built by string joining anywhere is enough, which makes this a property of the least careful line rather than of the codebase.

cost.time: dynamic queries need more care to express, and identifier cases need an explicit permitted set
cost.beats: escaping and filtering, which require no change to how queries are built and fail to one input nobody enumerated, and refusing unusual characters, which breaks legitimate names and still misses encodings

worked.problem: Why is filtering input an inadequate defence, and what makes parameterised queries different in kind?
worked.reasoning:
Because filtering accepts the dangerous situation and tries to survive it, while parameterisation removes the situation.

Start with what the vulnerability actually is, since the examples make it look like a problem about quote marks. A query built by joining fixed text to a supplied value produces one string, and the database cannot tell which parts came from the program and which from a stranger. If the stranger's contribution contains characters the language treats as structure rather than content, the stranger has written part of the query. The flaw is the combining, not the characters.

Filtering tries to identify hostile values before they are combined — strip dangerous characters, reject known attack patterns, escape what looks risky. It is appealing because it bolts onto an existing system without changing how queries are built.

It fails for a reason independent of the filter's quality. A filter must enumerate what is dangerous; the attacker needs one thing it did not enumerate. The search space is large — alternative encodings, different character sets, case variation, nesting that survives a single pass of replacement, constructs specific to one database the author never used. Every filter is a claim to have thought of everything, tested by people whose job is finding the exception. And being nearly perfect provides nearly no protection, because one working input is all that is required. That asymmetry is the argument: defence must be exhaustive, attack must be lucky once.

Parameterisation is different in kind rather than degree. The query text goes to the database with placeholders, and the values go separately. The database parses and plans the statement before the values are attached, so by the time a value arrives the structure is already fixed. A value containing a quote, a semicolon or a complete statement changes nothing, because there is nothing left to change — it is data being placed into a slot in an existing plan.

So filtering tries to detect hostility, and parameterisation makes hostility irrelevant. The first is a judgement that can be wrong; the second is a structural property that holds for every input, including inputs nobody has imagined. That is why it is worth being firm that this is the only real fix, rather than the best of several options.

Two limits, since it gets treated as total. It protects values, not structure: a table or column name, or a sort direction, cannot be a parameter, so code building those from input is still vulnerable and needs to select from a fixed set of permitted values. And it is only in force where used — one query built by string joining anywhere in the system is enough, so this is a property of the least careful line rather than of the codebase, which means it is a review and tooling problem as much as a knowledge problem.

The principle generalises and is worth carrying: the fix for mixing instructions with data is never better inspection of the data, it is an interface where the two cannot be mixed. Which also tells you why the equivalent problem for a language model is so hard — there, one sequence of text carries both, and no such interface exists.

problem.practice: Search your codebase for query construction that joins strings, and separately for any place a table name, column name or sort direction comes from a request. The first list should be empty; the second needs a fixed set of permitted values, because parameters cannot help there.

beats.broke: A query built by joining program text to a supplied value produces one string, and the database cannot tell which parts came from the program — so a value containing structural characters becomes part of the query.
beats.fix: Send the statement and its values separately, so the database plans the statement before any value is attached and a value has nothing left to change.
beats.cost: It protects values and not structure, so identifiers and sort directions built from input still need a fixed permitted set — and it holds only where used, making it a property of the least careful line.

interview.q: Why is filtering input an inadequate defence, and what makes parameterised queries different in kind?
interview.trap: Treating parameterisation as a stronger filter. It performs no inspection at all — the value arrives after the statement is planned, so hostility becomes irrelevant rather than detected.
interview.answer:
Because filtering accepts the dangerous situation and tries to survive it, while parameterisation removes the situation.

What the vulnerability actually is matters here, since the examples make it look like a problem about quote marks.
